title: Memory-Mapped Caching in Go: mmap Mechanics, Page Fault Latency, and the Eviction Boundary Problem
description: How mmap-backed caches behave under OS page reclaim, why Go's GC doesn't see the memory, and where the design breaks under pressure.
linkedin_post:
Memory-mapped caching in Go is a legitimate production technique that gets misapplied more often than it gets used correctly.

The appeal is real: reads off warm pages are 50–200ns, the backing memory is off-heap so GC never scans it, and there's no network hop. For large static read indexes—feature stores, lookup tables, geolocation databases—it's materially faster than a cross-AZ Redis call.

The failure modes are less discussed:

→ The OS controls eviction. When a co-resident container allocates heavily, kswapd reclaims your file-backed pages without any signal to your process. The next access triggers a major fault at 200µs–2ms on EBS. Your P99 spikes and you have nothing in your application metrics that explains it.

→ File rotation via rename(2) does not update an existing mapping. The process silently serves stale data. You must Munmap, reopen, and remap—with a synchronized fallback during the window.

→ Slices into mmap regions are not heap-managed. If a goroutine holds a subslice past Munmap, you have a use-after-free that surfaces as a SIGBUS panic, not a clean error.

→ mlock pins pages but requires CAP_IPC_LOCK, consumes locked memory quota, and is frequently restricted in ECS/EKS environments. Do not assume it's available.

The decision isn't "mmap vs Redis." It's a five-part check: Does your working set fit in RAM with headroom? Can you tolerate remap coordination on rotation? Is your latency budget resilient to page fault variance? What's the container density on the host? Can you enforce strict slice lifetime contracts across your goroutine model?

When all five are favorable, the pattern eliminates allocator contention and GC pressure for read-heavy workloads in ways that heap-based caches cannot match. When they're not, the opacity of OS page reclaim produces latency anomalies that are genuinely hard to root-cause without kernel-level tooling.
